body:
# Halmoni: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Halmoni, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Halmoni to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **할머니**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Halmoni**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'hahl-MOH-nee' — A three-syllable Korean word with light aspiration on the first consonant. It is a common kinship term elevated to divine status in folk religion. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *halmoni* differs from the canonical *Halmoni* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Halmoni is less a single deity than a title that gathers female sacred power across Korean religion.  It overlaps with Samshin Halmoni in birth cults, with Seolmundae Halmang in Jeju landscape myth, and with household ancestor spirits in Confucian-influenced ancestral rites — where the dead grandmother becomes a protective presence only so long as the lineage continues to feed her at the rites.

And it never stopped working. Halmoni remains vivid in Korean family life through ancestral rites, folk painting, Jeju mythology, and popular media.  The story of Seolmundae Halmang is retold in Jeju tourism, children's books, and regional festivals; the Yeongdeung-gut at Chilmeori-dang is a UNESCO-listed rite performed to this day.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Halmoni** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Halmoni** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *halmoni* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Halmoni** stands at [/halmoni/](/halmoni/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 5 cited sources — Kendall, Laurel, Shamans, Housewives, and Other Restless Spirits (University of Hawaii Press, 1985)., Lee, Jung Young, Korean Shamanistic Rituals (Mouton, 1981)., National Folk Museum of Korea, Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Beliefs (2015)..
